AbstractText.Label: RATIONALE
AbstractText.content: Obesity is relatively common among individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). However, little is known about the association of obesity with severity of acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) and in-hospital mortality.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVES
AbstractText.content: To examine the association of obesity with severity markers of AECOPD and in-hospital mortality.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: This is a retrospective cohort study using population-based data - the 2012-2013 State Inpatient Databases - of seven US states (Arkansas, Florida, Iowa, Nebraska, New York, Utah, and Washington). We included patients (aged ≥40 years) hospitalized for AECOPD. The outcome measures were markers of acute severity - use of non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV), invasive mechanical ventilation, and hospital length-of-stay (LOS) - and in-hospital mortality. To examine the association between obesity and each outcome, we fit unadjusted and adjusted logistic regression models using generalized estimating equations to account for patient clustering within hospitals. In the adjusted models, we adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, primary payer, median household income, patient residence, hospitalization year, chronic comorbidities, and hospital state. In the sensitivity analysis, we used stabilized inverse probability weighting to estimate the causal relation of obesity with outcomes in this observational study.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Of 187,647 patients with hospitalization for AECOPD, 17% were obese. Obese patients had significantly higher risks of both NIPPV (12.0% vs 6.5%; adjusted OR 1.86 [95%CI 1.77-1.95] P<0.001) and invasive mechanical ventilation use (3.5% vs 2.8%; adjusted OR 1.13 [95%CI 1.04-1.22] P=0.003) compared to non-obese patients. Similarly, obese patients were more likely to have a hospital LOS of ≥4 days (57.9% vs 50.3%, adjusted OR 1.37 [95%CI 1.33-1.41] P<0.001). By contrast, obesity was significantly associated with lower in-hospital mortality compared to non-obesity (0.9% vs 1.4%; unadjusted OR 0.63 [95%CI 0.56-0.72] P<0.001). This association lost statistical significance after adjusting for potential confounders including comorbidities (adjusted OR 0.86 [95%CI 0.75-1.00] P=0.06). In the sensitivity analysis with stabilized inverse probability weighting, these results were consistent.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: In this population-based study of adults hospitalized with AECOPD, obesity was associated with increased use of noninvasive and invasive ventilation, increased hospital length of stay, but was not associated with increased in-hospital mortality.
